en: I do not know who this Maitreya is, nor what age he manifests himself in. A person from Mingzhou spread word that this fat monk eats wine and meat,
carries a cloth bag with him, and treats others with great contempt by showing them a paper-wrapped piece of excrement.
[The Master] said: "This is Maitreya’s inner court; this is Tuṣita Heaven. Its fragrance permeates the air, deluding the men and women here.
The former Magistrate of Putian was fond of coming and going with him and allowing messages to pass between them.
At that time, it was fortunate he did not encounter me. Had he encountered me, I would have asked him: 'What is he? I would have waited for him to take down his cloth [of concealment]."
The bag. With palms joined before him, [the Master] struck him over the head with a single blow. He asked, "Where does the fault lie? and was struck again.
[The Master] said, "The sack has been torn open; I shall teach him that he has no words left to answer.
Furthermore, I shall have those seventeen or eighteen young children all crying out, 'My head hurts! My head hurts! *Duh!* Preface by the Historian of Fangzhou.
A Brief Preface to the Old Monk of the Cloth Bag:
The Sage observes that the minds of sentient beings are themselves the wisdom of *prajñā*. The ocean of birth and death is the city of *nirvāṇa*. Yet, being mired in ignorance, they do not know this;
it must be swiftly revealed through the Way. Consider how Maitreya received the prediction from Śākyamuni Buddha to open the gates of liberation and save sentient beings in the final age.
Thus, he descended from Tuṣita Heaven and roamed through Siming. At every place he reached, he erected the banner of radiance; wherever he encountered people, he bestowed the flavor of nectar.

He performed Buddha-activities with his cloth bag and manifested the state of a youthful sage through his young son. His spiritual transformations in the four modes of conduct were unfathomable, and his wondrous edification throughout the six periods was inexhaustible.
Those who ascended into his meditation cave died their thieving minds at the point of ultimate liberation, yet revived their divine mechanisms.

At a time when it was difficult to explain, he therefore plucked a flower to reveal the essential meaning, a resonance that echoes through the ages. With a smile and a gesture of the hand, the needle and the magnet meet;
thus, one is made to let go of the sack and intuitively realize the profound mystery. This indeed requires no further words; those who seek it through thought will find it.

This is the purport of the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings. Alas! I consider this to be the words of an old monk in his final rebirth, appending superfluous remarks from a thousand or ten thousand years ago.
Written as a preface in humble homage by the layman Shen Yiguan.
I have heard that the Way of the sages and worthies is something each person possesses inherently; how could it be sought through external conditions?

It is merely because one is self-enclosed by worldly defilements and self-deluded regarding the other shore that one is needlessly cast down into the midst of birth and death and adrift amidst the cycles of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, O Ajita, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni bestowed upon you the prediction of the Buddha Vehicle and entrusted to you the affairs of the Buddha; thus, the journey ahead is ten thousand...
This chapter comprehensively encompasses the entire school. It reveals the Truth through delusion and clarifies the Principle through phenomena.
It gathers all the Buddha-dharmas into a single sack and wields immeasurable supernatural powers within the palm of the hand.

It seeks directly to overturn the karmic consciousness and causal conditions accumulated by all people since beginningless kalpas, to sever the very root of birth and death, and to achieve a thorough realization of non-arising.

The wisdom of nature (*xingzhi*) is precisely the realization that the entire body is Amitābha and that the Pure Land is solely the mind. It is merely a matter of the single point of delusion versus awakening.
Thus, the Transmission says: "This very mind, mind after mind, is the Buddha; it is the most wondrous and sentient thing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Its transverse and vertical wondrous functions are truly pitiable; nothing else compares to the reality of this mind. How true these words are!
The lay practitioner Dazhen Bao Shiyin of Yongshang read the *Biography of Maitreya* one hundred times.
Having attained the essential flavor of Chan through discussions with Master Changji, he composed several lines of verse and inscribed them on the First Pavilion of Yaoguang.
The Biography of Master Pùdàng of Dìngyīng in Míngzhōu:
The Master was a man of unknown origins. During the Liáng period of the Five Dynasties, he appeared in Fènghuà County, Míngzhōu.
He had a furrowed brow and a protruding belly; his physique was stout and fleshy. No one in the world knew his clan, family name, or given name; he always referred to himself as Qìchǐ.
As for Changtingzi and Pudu Huashang, they were so named according to what people observed.
Day and night, they had no fixed place for sleeping or eating, yet E’lin Temple was where they would invariably stay.
They always carried a monk’s staff and a cloth bag with them, and eighteen young boys followed them with great care; however, it was never known from where these boys came.
While traveling through villages and fields, he saw pickled fish and fermented vegetables. He would immediately beg for eight mouthfuls, placing the remainder into his bag.
Upon reaching a marketplace, he opened the bag and emptied its contents all at once, saying to the crowd, "Look! Look!
Then, picking them up one by one, he asked the people, "Tell me, what is this? After doing this for a long while, he put them back into the bag and carried it away.
He would go about constantly carrying a paper-wrapped object that looked like excrement, showing it to people and saying, "This is the Inner Court of Maitreya.
At other times he would say, "This is the Heaven of the Tuṣita Court. Once, as a monk was walking slowly ahead of him, the Master patted the monk on the back.
The monk turned his head and asked, "What are you doing? The Master extended his hand and said, "Give me one coin. The monk replied, "If you can speak [the right words], then..."
[The Master] gave it to him. The teacher set down his cloth bag and stood with hands folded. One day, while staying among a crowd of people, a monk asked, "What are you doing here, Master?
The teacher said, "I am waiting for someone. The monk said, "What about me? The teacher reached into his breast.
He took out an orange and gave it to him. As the monk reached out to receive it, the Master withdrew his hand and said, "You are not that kind of person.
Later, as the Master was standing casually in the marketplace, a monk asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "Soliciting alms. The monk said:
"What kind of conditions do you seek to transform at the crossroads? The Master said, "At the crossroads, it is precisely where one should seek alms.
As the monk hesitated, the Master slung his hemp bag over his shoulder, laughed loudly, and departed. Later, Monk Bailu asked, "What is this hemp bag?"
The Master set down his cloth bag, stood with his hands folded, and asked, "What is the matter beneath the cloth bag?
The Master took up the cloth bag and walked away. Baofu Wenheshang asked, "What is the very meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master set down the cloth bag and stood there. Baofu asked, "Is it only this? Is there more? The Master took up the cloth bag and walked away. Or...
A new latrine was recently constructed in the marketplace. The Master stood before it and proclaimed, "This has been built through the solicitation of offerings;
one must not perform the two functions [of nature] here. Wherever the Master went for alms, people would immediately detain and pull him back, refusing to let him leave.

Even at wine shops and butcher stalls, they all allowed him to drink and eat to his heart's content, feeling no sense of revulsion, believing that this would cause their goods to sell twice as well and yield great profits.
If he encountered rain, he would rise at dawn, put on high-toothed wooden clogs, and lie down with his legs extended across a large bridge; on that day, it would certainly be sunny.
If he encountered sunshine, he would tie on straw sandals and run about; on that day, it would certainly rain. The Master once planted mugwort throughout his fields.
The following year, the government issued an edict to increase taxes and the corvée labor quota for able-bodied men. As a result, the common people fled, and the fields fell into total ruin.

Once, the Master went to a farming household for a meal; the wife, in a fit of anger, reviled her husband, saying, "In the midst of the busy farming season, how can you afford to worry about this wind-swept monk?
The Master immediately poured out his food beneath a mulberry tree and departed. Shortly thereafter, the food was found back inside the cooking pot.
Wei Xun said: "When he was asked to perform penance, he bathed in a mountain stream during the summer. He took off his clothes and placed them on the bank;

a group of children played there, gathered the clothes, and ran away. The Master stripped naked and pursued them. People on the bank gathered to watch, and they secretly beheld his private organ; it was indeed that of a true youth."
There was a land-dweller who was skilled at painting; he had depicted the Master’s likeness on the wall of the monastery’s storehouse. When the Master passed by it, he spat incessantly.

While the Master was in Min, there was a layman named Chen who hosted him with great care. Later, when the Master traveled through the two Zhe provinces and took his leave of him, the layman asked, "What is your surname, Master?
On what day and month were you born? How many years have you been in the Dharma? The Master replied:
"Do not say that I am surnamed Li. I was born on the eighth day of the second month. This very cloth bag has been of the same age as empty space.
The layman then said to the Master, "If anyone asks you this when you go from here, answer only in this way;
do not fall into the disputes of others. The Master replied with a verse: "In this world, likes, dislikes, and attachments abound. Reflect upon them carefully..."
"What can they do to me? I shall broaden my belly and constantly practice forbearance; I shall let go and allow the days to pass away in quiet consumption.
If I meet a true friend, I shall act according to the proper measure; even if I encounter an enemy, I shall harmonize with them.
To ensure this mind is free from obstruction, one will naturally realize the six *pāramitās*. He asked again, "Does the Master have a Dharma name? The Master replied once more with a verse:
I have a cloth bag; empty space is without obstruction. When opened, it pervades the ten directions; at all eight watches, Avalokiteśvara is present.
He asked again, "Do you have any provisions for the journey? He replied with a verse: "A single bowl for the meals of a thousand households; a solitary body wandering ten thousand li."
Seeing that a person’s blue eyes remain, he asks the way at the head of the white clouds. He asks again: "I, your disciple, am ignorant and dull-witted;
how may I come to see the Buddha-nature? In verse, [the Master] replies: "This very mind is the Buddha; it is the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions."
"His wondrous functions, traversing all directions, are truly pitiable; nothing compares to the reality of the mind. He further said, "When you go, Master, you must stay in a temple;
do not dwell in reliance upon a lay household. The Master replied with a verse: "I have a hall of the Three Jewels."
Within, it is empty and devoid of form; neither high nor low, without obstruction or hindrance. Those who study cannot grasp its essence; those who seek find no model to emulate.
Only the wise understand how to arrange it; throughout the ages, not a single craftsman has appeared. Thus, the four gates give rise to the four fruits.

The layman made offerings throughout the ten directions, yet he found this extraordinary. He prostrated once more and said, "I pray that the Master will remain for another night of meals, so that I may fully express my disciple’s intent of reverence. That evening, the Master again wrote a verse upon the layman’s gate, saying:
"I have a Buddha-body, Which the people of the world do not recognize. It is neither molded nor adorned; It is neither carved nor..."
It is carved; yet there is not a single piece of clay, nor a trace of color. A master painter could not create it, and a thief could not steal it away.
Its form and characteristics are fundamentally natural; it is pure and eternally radiant. Although it is but a single body, it manifests as hundreds of billions of emanations.
Upon arriving at Siming, he associated with the local man Jiang Zongba; their interactions regarding conduct, dwelling, and meals were especially intimate.
He instructed him to take the recitation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* as his daily practice;
consequently, the world came to call Zongba the "Mahā Layman. One day, while bathing in the Changting Stream, he had Mahā scrub his back.
Suddenly, he saw four eyes on the Master’s back, shining with a brilliant, dazzling light. Startled and awestruck, Mahā prostrated himself and said, "The Master is a Buddha!"
The Master said, "Do not speak of this. I have been with you for three or four years; it can be said that we share a great karmic affinity.
I am about to leave you, so do not grieve. He then went to Mahā’s house and said to him gently, "Do you desire wealth and honor?
Mahā replied, "How could wealth and honor endure forever? I only wish that my descendants may endure for a long time. The Master then—
Taking a cloth bag containing countless small items, along with a chest and a rope, he handed them to Mahā, saying, "I give these things to you as my parting gift;
they concern your future generations. Having received them, Mahā did not understand their significance.
After several days, the Master returned and asked, "Do you understand my meaning? Mahā replied, "Your disciple does not understand."
The Master said, "This is because I wish for your descendants to be like the objects I have left behind.
On the third day of the third month in the third year of the Zhengming era, he manifested his passing on a flat rock beneath the eaves of Yuelin Temple.

While the Master was still in good health, the village head of Zhen, finding him to be negligent in his duties, would frequently insult and humiliate him; furthermore, he seized the Master’s bag and burned it. The following day, the Master carried [the remains]...
[The Master] took a sack; his coming and going were as they had been before. This occurred three times, and each time it returned to its former state.
Although even the village headman marveled at this in his heart, when it came time to purchase a coffin for the enshrinement, [the body] could not be lifted despite a great number of bearers.

There was a man of the Tong family who had long revered the Master; he exchanged his own coffin for it. Though the number of bearers did not increase, it was lifted as lightly as a feather. Thereupon, throughout the land—
A great assembly was convened, and a stupa was erected on the plain of Fengshan. That mountain consists entirely of rocky cliffs;
the hollows and caves within the rocks are all traces left by the Great Master. There is the place where he planted his mendicant’s staff, and the place where he set down his alms bowl.

The pit where the bowl was placed is exactly as deep, shallow, small, or large as the bowl itself, yet water always fills it to the brim. Even during a great drought, it does not diminish; this is truly marvelous.
Ten years after [the Master] had passed away, a messenger from the army of Yue was returning to Shu via the Zigzag Road (Zhandao).
Upon seeing the Master there, he recognized him and said, "There is one named Jang Mahā at Siming; please convey my regards to him and ask that he preserve his health until we may meet again.
At that time, Mahā was building a hermitage on the steep heights of the Twelve Terraces of Mount Bangu.
He lived in seclusion, keeping a yellow dog for his own protection. Whenever his rice was exhausted, he would tie one hundred coins around the dog’s neck and go to Eastern Wu to purchase more;
he traveled back and forth twenty *li* without interruption. When the envoy from Shu arrived with the imperial summons, Mahā said, "I already knew this.
He immediately prepared a vegetarian feast for his relatives and friends, bathed, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. This occurred during the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty.
First, Wang Renxu, the Magistrate of Putian County in Xinghua Commandery, met the Great Master at Tianxing Temple in Jiangnan.

Later, they met again at the official residence in Fuzhou. [The Master] produced a sealed scroll from his breast and instructed Wang, saying: "If I do not return within seven days, then open it to read.
Wang followed these instructions faithfully; upon opening the sealed scroll, there were no other words, only a single verse. The verse:

It says: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; his emanations number in the hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions. From time to time he manifests to the people of the world, yet the people do not recognize him.
Below this, nine characters state: "One must not attempt to depict my likeness; this [likeness] is the true one. Upon reaching this point, one then knows that the Master was indeed Maitreya Buddha.
In the third year of the Xining era of the Song dynasty (1070 CE), the descendant Yi Sun-zu of Putian was still able to treasure it.
The original manuscript. The following year, Liu Jiyè of Jìn'ān transcribed its verse text and also painted an image of the Great Master, carving them into stone at Yíchūn;
however, nine characters were omitted. In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era, the śramaṇa Zōngshàng obtained this copy.

It was carved as a replica behind Yue-lin Temple. Three years later, Lü Zhen of Wenling, serving as the Superintendent of Maritime Trade for Mingzhou, produced the authentic nine-character original manuscript preserved by his descendants from Putian. He commissioned the abbot Ru-xun to carve it after the verse.
Ru-xun, considering that illusory forms were not the Great Master’s intent, ordered them removed. Consequently, the verse was moved to the stone, and the nine characters were inscribed alongside it.

This was passed down by tradition. As for Lu Shiqi, he once served as the magistrate of this county; he held him in particularly high esteem and veneration, commissioning an artist to paint his portrait.

He then had it brought to the Eight-County Office (Baxian-shu) for worship, whereupon wind and rain would follow its presence. His prayers were exceptionally efficacious, and the incense offerings have continued to this day.
Furthermore, someone saw him on the road to Dongyang, carrying a single shoe and saying to the person: "In the past, I mistakenly took [this]."
"From this point forward, you may now take this with you and return home. Later, when you open the tomb to look within, indeed there will remain only a single shoe.
The Master composed many verses and hymns; here, I shall briefly record one or two to serve as a warning to the world. He said:
"Vigorous and free, acting without purpose, Tranquil and at ease, the ultimate child of the renunciant life. If you behold the Great Way before your eyes, You will see nothing [else]."
How truly marvelous, even a single hair! How can the myriad dharmas differ from the mind? Why labor further to seek the meaning of the scriptures?
The Mind-King is inherently beyond manifold knowledge. The wise simply clarify the stage of no-more-learning; how could it be anything other than neither-saint-nor-ordinary?
Not forcing discrimination, the Sage’s sentiment is solitary; the priceless jewel of the mind is fundamentally round and pure. All that are perceived as disparate forms are but empty delusions.
It is man who can propagate the Way, for the Way is clearly manifest. Immeasurable purity and loftiness are what one calls the sentiment of the Way.

Carrying your staff, if you should ascend the roads of your former kingdom, do not worry that the sound will not be heard in all places. Afterward, a master of arts said to people: "Two hundred years..."
Later, the Dharma site of Yue-lin Temple, where the Baguā Monk resided, was restored.

During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, the abbot Yuanming—successor to Zhaojue of Donglin and descendant of the layman Chen of Fuzhou—renewed the temple’s mountain enclosures, pagodas, and pavilions.
Feng Sidao and others further donated surrounding land to expand its foundations. Suddenly, [a vision] appeared...

A strange light appeared. Upon digging, they obtained a yellow-colored pure flask (*śuci-ghaṭa*) and a six-ringed mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), both of exquisite and ancient craftsmanship. Onlookers sighed in admiration.

The officials reported this matter to the throne. On the ninth day of the sixth month of the Wuyin year of the Kaiyuan era of the Yuanchu period, an imperial edict was issued bestowing his current posthumous title.
In the third year of the Chongning era, the abbot Tanzhen exhorted the local personage, the Dong family, to construct a pavilion behind the temple.
A local personage, the Ren family, fashioned a statue of the Master and placed it within the pavilion.

Subsequently, the Dong family, asserting that they had built the pavilion, commissioned their own statue and installed it upon it, moving the Ren family statue to the base of the pavilion. [There was a practitioner of arts...]
One person said, "The image of the Dong family [enshrined] will last for only sixty years; the image of the Ren family will exceed sixty years before its fortune begins to unfold.
When the temple was consumed by fire during the Shaoxing era, the pavilion was completely destroyed along with it, and the image of the Dong family was reduced to ashes.
At that time, there was a man of abundant spiritual power who, having healed one arm, traveled for alms and, while traveling with a śramaṇa, rebuilt the pavilion.

He then invited the statue of Lady Ren and placed it upon it; pointing his finger, he counted [the years], and the words of the practitioner were indeed proven true. This occurred at the beginning of the Jiatai era.
The structure of the pavilion was on the verge of collapsing. One night, wind and rain broke out suddenly, and thunder and lightning struck together. At dawn, it stood firm and upright once more;

moreover, between the beams and rafters, there were traces of scales, shells, duckweed, and algae all over. Chan Master Zhao of Huaihai composed a stele inscription for this event to marvel at the power of divine assistance.
When the Yuan Dynasty arrived, the pavilion collapsed in the ninth month of the nineteenth year of Zhizong.
On the ninth day of the month, the Master’s portrait alone remained undamaged; his majestic features stood tall amidst the rubble.

Furthermore, the standing image on the altar was able to leap into the bamboo grove of the rear garden. Nobles and commoners from near and far ceased their work and closed their markets to pay homage, gaze upon it, and express their profound admiration.
In the eighteenth year, while residing at the mountain monastery, Fan Zhong-lin selected a worthy successor to continue the construction of the five [halls].
Its scale is magnificent, and all who behold it marvel at its grandeur. Furthermore, it enshrines the image carved by the Ren clan;
such is its manifest trace. As for its essence, however, it exists throughout every dust mote and world-system, remaining imperishable through kalpas as numerous as grains of sand.

Since this is the case regarding his primary retribution (*vipāka*), it is likewise with his secondary environment (*niśraya-vipāka*). Were it not for the Great Master, to whom could we turn for refuge?
This was composed by the monk Tan’uo, known as Wumeng, the incumbent of Guoqing Chan Monastery in the former Tiantai region.
This is the postscript to the *Puduo Heshang* (Baguān).
I reverently hear that the Dharma-body is formless, yet it encompasses all numerical forms; that the nature of awakening is unborn, so how could it be hindered by thoughts of arising and ceasing?
All worlds are like space, and the five aggregates of body and mind are unreal. Because they are unreal, they are like space.

Therefore, the world is the Dharmadhātu of Vairocana; the aggregates and the mind are the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). Throughout kalpas it is unborn, and through ten thousand ages it is unextinguished.
It is vast and profound, tranquil and luminous. This is the ultimate fruit of Bodhi realized equally by all Tathāgatas and all sentient beings.
It is only because they have not yet awakened to their own true nature that they delusively cling to illusory appearances and remain immersed in them.
In this sea of suffering, beings take up saṃsāra for themselves. Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the sūtras and the Three Jewels fill the world.

If one maintains faith and practice with diligence, it is as if the Buddha were still present in the world. Yet, for those of shallow wisdom and deep obstructions, he is as distant as a thousand li even when facing him directly;

thus, the Sage cannot but descend to the human realm to deliver all ordinary beings. What was anciently called the Land of the Four Ming Mountains and the Three Buddhas refers to the past Buddha Vipaśyin.
The Buddha manifested the appearance of a mute girl and transformed her through his gentle wisdom and virtue.

Śākyamuni Tathāgata distributed his *śarīra* relics and specifically emitted light and displayed auspicious omens to benefit sentient beings; these accounts of the three Buddhas are recorded in detail.

As for the World-Honored One Maitreya, who succeeds to the position of Śākyamuni Buddha, he delivers sentient beings according to the ritual forms. As stated in the *Guan yinguo jing*: "Śākyamuni Buddha... [text continues].
The lineage of Kāśyapa Buddha’s Dharma has always resided in Tuṣita Heaven, where he is known as the Bodhisattva Maitreya.

Responding to the opportune moment, he descended to be born, turned the Great Wheel of Dharma, and brought vast salvation to the myriad species, universally benefiting beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

He was once prophesied as the fifth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa; thus he is called the "Successor" (Upapadya). This does not mean he succeeds the seat of Gautama Buddha, but rather that he succeeds Śākyamuni in the celestial palace.

He still resides in the Tuṣita Heaven, known as the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Although he dwells in the Tuṣita Palace, he manifests transformation bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions, out of compassion for the sentient beings of the nine realms within the trichiliocosm. Whether they are cultivating the six perfections and myriad practices, or indulging in the three poisons and four inversions;
whether they are creating the deep causes for the hells, or planting the minor fruits of humans and devas—it is for their sake that he performs these great deeds.

Providing shelter and universal transformation through his benevolent influence: once, during the Xiao-Liang period of the Six Dynasties, he manifested his traces at Yiwu as the Great Being (Mahāsattva) Fu;

there he established a *dharma-hall* at Shuanglin, and his *Shuanglin Yulu* remains extant for the world. Once, during the Xizong reign of the late Tang dynasty, he appeared spontaneously in Siming as the Cloth Bag Monk;
with his belly bared and a smile upon his face, he concealed his virtue as if he were a fool, ultimately [never revealing it].
One knows him to be a man of such caliber: his appearance was not adorned with formal grace, and he lived in the world with few conventional norms.
Yet, his utterances were vast as heaven and earth, and his martial bearing was neither saintly nor ordinary. He was substantial rather than hollow, and natural rather than contrived.

He constantly had eighteen youths surrounding him as if in play, manifesting supernatural powers through the mutual interaction of the sense faculties and their objects to purify wisdom. He always maintained [his practice of] *fubo* (wearing coarse cloth).
The Bag: This reveals the fundamental principles of the Buddha’s school. It encompasses immeasurable secret causes and brings forth boundless, wondrous functions.

For those in the world who follow their own whims in binding their karma and pursue their desires with extreme greed, the Master, according to their respective conditions, provides harmonious guidance and progressively awakens them to clarity.
He causes those at that place to uphold benevolence and righteousness, realizing that delusion is itself truth.

Or, in places where people wander for alms, seeing those who contend over paths of greedy profit and are mired in the river of craving, the Master uses harmonious and gentle speech to unlock their fetters.

Pointing toward the essential pivot, he speaks directly of awakened wisdom according to their individual capacities, exhorting them to sever the dust-like habits of worldly life and melt away the influence of heterodox winds, so that every person may be transformed.

The Dharma bestows grace, much like the springtime of the green willows. When encountering a seeker of the Way, it is essential that the virtuous teacher brings about the realization of one’s own perfect, enlightened, and luminous nature.
This luminosity is vast and unobstructed; this unobstructed state is the unmoving True Suchness (*tathatā*). This True Suchness is continuous and without interval;
being without interval, it is all-pervasive, perfectly interfused, and perfectly harmonious. Being perfectly harmonious, it is liberation and sovereign mastery; being sovereign, it is without...

Whether it be acceptable or not, he spoke of the profound mystery with ease. Those who transcended emotion and severed conceptual understanding, realizing the essence of the Way, each had their minds opened and their wisdom purified, like the bright sun shining in the sky.
When the Master traveled northward, he saw a butcher slaughtering livestock and admonished him, saying:

"All these animals are the karmic retribution of those who committed evil deeds. If you desire the Way but lack the means to do so, you can save them. I pray that all you elders will spare these lives."
Living beings—teach them how to sustain their lives. All wriggling and sentient creatures possess Buddha-nature; O Benevolent One, you should regard them with eyes of compassion.
This is not only the virtue of benefiting others through mercy, but it further plants the seeds for Bodhi and longevity.

Furthermore, he encountered a butcher who said: "The one who kills a cow is called a *rātri* (a night-roamer); when killing another, who is it that feels terror? [They stand upon] mountains of knives and axes."
"From the time of frying in a pan, through what kalpa and at what time shall one attain liberation? A monk asked, "How does one subdue the deluded mind?

The Master said, "What thing is this 'mind'? To laboriously strive to subdue it is in vain. Delusion has no root; let it go and there will be no trace. Amidst the turmoil of all conditions," [the mind remains as it is].

The One Truth is serene and still; the body of the *tathatā* dharma-realm is majestic and grand. It cannot be split by the axe, nor obscured by darkness. The Master pointed to a monk of worldly habits and said:
"You are originally a Buddha. Why do you linger in ordinary sentiments? You must sever all external conditions and wash away the dust of habitual tendencies.
Exert yourself to investigate the unborn nature of the mind and realize the wondrously luminous true essence. If you attain unimpeded, perfect penetration, then—"

"This is an Arhat who has transcended the dust of the world; otherwise, it would be a waste to kill such a man. The Master was receiving a vegetarian feast from a farming family when he asked a question.
The host replied: "The ox treads upon the green seedlings to plant the field of merit; by lowering one's head, one immediately sees the sky reflected in the water.

When the six sense organs are purified, only then does the rice ripen; retreating backward is originally moving forward. Later, while the Master sat at night on a large bridge, a violent man suddenly appeared.
He peered inside. The Master said, "I, this poor monk, have no wealth; you, sir, have likewise no delusion. Why do you covet wealth and profit, thereby obscuring your own wondrous clarity?
From kalpa after kalpa since birth, you have been misled by greed and have suffered in vain through the cycle of rebirth. Why do you not reflect on this? You harbor thoughts of theft in secret."

The Biography of the Baguā Monk.
The Monk Pùtí of Fènghuà in Míngzhōu was a man of unknown origins. He called himself Qìchǐ, and his clan and family name remained obscure.
His physical form was stout and fleshy; he had a furrowed brow and a protruding belly. His speech was unpredictable, and he would sleep wherever he happened to be.
He constantly carried a staff upon which he slung a cloth bag and a tattered mat. All the implements necessary for his livelihood were stored within that bag.

He entered the marketplaces and villages; whenever he saw something, he would beg for it—be it vinegar, fermented soybeans, fish, or pickled vegetables. As soon as it reached his mouth, he would take a small portion and place it in his bag.
At that time, he was called Changtingzi (The Man of the Long Embankment). One day, a monk was walking ahead of him, and the Master patted the monk on the back.

The monk said, "He has come! He has come! Guizong Rouniuzhi added, "Go back! Go back! The Master said, "You are not that person. The monk said, "..."
"What is this person? The Master said, "Ask me for one coin. The Master had a song which said: "This very mind—mind is Buddha;
it is the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions. Its transverse and vertical wondrous functions are truly pitiable;
nothing compares to the reality of the mind. Soaring freely and at ease, there is nothing to do; leisurely and ultimate, such is the child who has left the home-life. If...
Beholding the true Great Way before one’s eyes, not seeing even a hair’s breadth—how truly marvelous! How can the myriad dharmas differ, and how can the mind be otherwise?
Why labor further to seek the meaning of the scriptures? The Sovereign Mind is inherently free from manifold knowledge; the wise simply clarify the stage of no-learning.
Neither saint nor ordinary person, it is again as level as a plain. Not forcing discrimination, the sagely sentiment is solitary. The priceless jewel of the mind is fundamentally...

Perfectly Pure. All that has distinct characteristics is called empty delusion. A person can propagate the Way; when the Way is clearly understood, its immeasurable purity and loftiness accord with the Way-seeking mind.
Carrying your staff as you walk the roads of your former country, do not worry that you will not hear the sound where you seek it.
There is also a verse that says: "In this world, likes, dislikes, attachments, and aversions abound. Reflect carefully upon this—what can they do to me? One must broaden one's heart and belly..."
Patience: Open up the ground of your mind and let things take their course. If you meet a true friend, follow the natural measure; even if you encounter an enemy, remain in harmony.
If you can resolve this matter within your heart, you will naturally realize the six pāramitās.
I have a cloth bag, empty and unobstructed like space; when spread out, it pervades the ten directions, yet when entering, one is Avalokiteśvara. I have three...
The Precious Hall is empty within, devoid of form or appearance; it is neither high nor low, neither obstructed nor hindered.

Those who study it find no likeness to its essence; those who come find it difficult to grasp its model. Only through wisdom can one understand how to arrange it—among a thousand, there is not a single craftsman.
From its four gates, the four fruits arise; the ten directions all offer worship. I have a Buddha-body, yet the people of the world do not recognize it; it is neither modeled nor sculpted.
It is not adorned; it is neither carved nor engraved. There is not a single drop of plaster, nor a speck of color.
A person may try to paint it but cannot succeed; a thief may try to steal it but cannot take it. Its physical form is inherently natural; its purity requires no wiping away.

Although it is but a single body, it manifests in hundreds of thousands of millions of forms. Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "A single bowl for the meals of a thousand households; a solitary body across ten thousand *li*."

Wandering, he beheld few people in the blue distance and asked for the way at the head of the white clouds. In the third month of the Bingzi year, the third year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty, the Master was about to manifest his passing.
At the eastern corridor of Yuelin Temple, he sat upright upon a large rock and spoke this verse:

"Maitreya is truly Maitreya, Manifesting a thousand, ten thousand, and ten million bodies. From time to time he shows himself to those of the age, Yet the people of the age do not recognize him themselves. Thus ends the verse.
He passed away peacefully; subsequently, he reappeared in another province, likewise walking while carrying a cloth bag on his back.
The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his likeness.
